claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by differential elemental diffusion that produces a self-healing, adherent oxide scale enriched in refractory, low-diffusivity elements.
Solution treatment produces a homogenized multiprincipal-element alloy with a uniform elemental distribution.
A controlled comparison should test a standard alloy against variants containing increased fractions of refractory or glassy oxide-forming elements.
Ta can serve as a refractory or glassy oxide-forming addition that improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The comparison should cover 800–1200 °C under identical oxidizing atmospheres using both isothermal and cyclic exposures.
The modified alloys will form a protective passive scale selectively enriched in refractory, slow-diffusing elements.
A scale incorporating glass-forming species can act as a dense, viscous barrier against oxygen ingress.
At high temperature, low-mobility elements such as Ta preferentially segregate to the alloy surface because of differential diffusion.
Oxidation of the surface-segregated refractory elements produces a stable, adherent passive oxide that slows further oxidation and preserves bulk integrity.
Alloys enriched in refractory or glassy oxide-formers will develop thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scales than the baseline alloys.
The modified alloys will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain than the baseline alloys.
The modified alloys will retain their mechanical properties better after oxidation than the baseline alloys.
The proposed diffusion-controlled relationship should remain valid from 800 °C to 1200 °C.
Outside 800–1200 °C, different oxidation kinetics or phase transformations may cause deviations from the proposed relationship.
Predictions of diffusion behavior and oxide-phase composition require calibration against experimental measurements.
Failure of the modified alloys to improve oxide thickness, weight gain, mechanical-property retention, or the predicted segregation–oxide correlation would falsify the hypothesis.
